slides.title: Replicating Your Best Stores
slides.subtitle: A 30 / 60 / 90 day path to reduce variance across 120 APAC stores
slides.script: We believe the opportunity at RetailCo is not to chase an abstract average. It is to find what already works inside your best stores, make it visible, and replicate it consistently across the network. You have 120 stores, 2,000 frontline staff, and a three-times gap between your strongest and weakest store managers. That tells us the answer is already in the business. Our proposal is to capture the signals, codify the winning behaviors, and turn them into an operating system your teams can actually use.

slides.title: The scale makes variance expensive
slides.script: We start with the scale because it changes the shape of the problem. At 120 stores, small differences in manager routines, floor coverage, customer conversations, and onboarding habits do not stay small. Across 2,000 frontline staff, those differences become the operating reality customers experience every day. The three-times gap between your best and worst store managers is the signal that matters most. It says RetailCo does not lack talent or know-how. The challenge is that the know-how is trapped locally, unevenly transferred, and often invisible until a Monday spreadsheet arrives.

slides.text: RetailCo’s biggest opportunity is reducing variance by replicating what your best managers already do.
slides.script: We would frame this as a variance problem, not a performance problem. Average performance can hide the fact that some stores have already solved the operating questions others are struggling with. Your best managers know how to deploy people, coach a sales conversation, read the shop floor, and bring new hires up to speed. Today, that knowledge is carried in habits and judgment. Our job is to make those patterns observable, comparable, and teachable, so the network can learn from its own best examples rather than relying on generic playbooks.

slides.title: 30 / 60 / 90: from visibility to replication

steps.label: 30 days
steps.text: See and hear real store behavior with Spacesight and Echo.

steps.label: 60 days
steps.text: Bottle best-practice routines inside Harbor Wiki.

steps.label: 90 days
steps.text: Package the operating proposal with Alivia and define scheduling next steps.

slides.script: We are proposing a three-horizon plan because each horizon answers a different question. In the first 30 days, we establish what is really happening in stores, not what appears in a delayed spreadsheet. In the next 60 days, we compare the behaviors of stronger and weaker stores and bottle the practices that deserve to travel. By 90 days, we turn that into a practical proposal, supported by Alivia, and we are explicit about scheduling. The current product set informs that pain, but it does not fully solve rostering by itself.

slides.title: Each COO pain mapped to the right response

rows.right: Spacesight shows what happens in-store before Monday.
Spacesight plus Echo identify what best managers do differently.
Harbor Wiki turns proven routines into searchable guidance.
Open item: discovery maps workflow, handoffs, and integration options.
Alivia turns the findings into a client-ready proposal.

slides.script: We want to be very clear about coverage. Spacesight directly answers the visibility problem by showing what is happening on the shop floor. Echo adds the customer conversation layer, so we can hear how staff actually sell, explain, and recover. Harbor Wiki addresses the onboarding and replication issue by turning best practice into something searchable and repeatable. Alivia helps convert the combined findings into a coherent proposal. Scheduling is different. The products can reveal demand patterns and coordination pain, but a roster engine is an open item for discovery, not something we should pretend is solved.

slides.title: First 30 days: make the floor observable

steps.label: Instrument
steps.text: Deploy Spacesight in selected stores to capture floor activity.

steps.label: Listen
steps.text: Use Echo to capture and score customer conversations.

steps.label: Compare
steps.text: Contrast strong and weak stores on observable behaviors.

steps.label: Read out
steps.text: Show same-week signals instead of waiting for Monday.

slides.script: In the first 30 days, we focus on replacing hindsight with visibility. Your current pain is very specific: you get a spreadsheet on Monday about last week. Spacesight changes that by making floor activity observable during the week. Echo complements it by showing what frontline staff actually say to customers, not just whether a sale happened. We would select a practical store sample, including high and low performers, and compare behaviors side by side. The output is not a dashboard for its own sake; it is the first evidence base for replication.

slides.title: How signals become standards

steps.label: Observe
steps.text: Capture real store and conversation patterns.

steps.label: Identify
steps.text: Find behaviors that separate stronger managers.

steps.label: Codify
steps.text: Write those behaviors into usable store guidance.

steps.label: Reinforce
steps.text: Use the guidance in onboarding and coaching.

slides.script: The important move is that we do not stop at observation. A camera feed or conversation score is only useful if it climbs the ladder into a standard. First, we observe what is actually happening. Then we identify which behaviors correlate with the stores and managers you already trust. Next, we codify those behaviors in plain language, so they are not trapped in one manager’s head. Finally, we reinforce them through onboarding and coaching. That is how we move from insight to a repeatable operating habit across the network.

slides.title: Next 60 days: bottle the best managers

steps.label: Select
steps.text: Choose routines worth copying from high-performing stores.

steps.label: Write
steps.text: Create Harbor Wiki pages for common store moments.

steps.label: Train
steps.text: Use the wiki in new-hire and manager coaching.

steps.label: Refresh
steps.text: Update guidance as new patterns emerge.

slides.script: By day 60, the focus shifts from finding differences to spreading what works. Harbor Wiki becomes the place where RetailCo bottles the habits of its best managers. That might include how they open a shift, coach a slow hour, handle a product question, or guide a new hire through the first customer interaction. This directly addresses your onboarding concern: today it takes six weeks and depends on whoever happens to be working that day. The wiki gives every store a common reference point, while still allowing local managers to contribute what proves effective.

slides.title: The operating shift RetailCo should feel

rows.right: Winning routines are visible and teachable

rows.left: Onboarding depends on who is working
rows.right: New hires use shared Harbor Wiki guidance
Discovery defines workflow, data, and integration needs

slides.script: This is the practical change we are aiming for. Instead of learning on Monday what happened last week, leaders can see patterns while they are still actionable. Instead of accepting that one manager outsells another by three times without knowing why, we can isolate the behaviors worth copying. Instead of new hires receiving different training depending on the shift they join, they get a shared source of truth. And on scheduling, we separate evidence from automation. We can map the handoffs and demand signals, then determine what tooling or integration is required.

slides.title: By 90 days: turn the learning into a decision

steps.label: Validate
steps.text: Confirm which behaviors and signals leaders trust.

steps.label: Package
steps.text: Use Alivia to shape the proposal and options.

steps.label: Decide
steps.text: Agree the rollout path across APAC stores.

slides.script: By 90 days, we should not just have observations; we should have a decision-ready proposal. Alivia helps package the evidence, recommended rollout path, and practical operating changes into a proposal RetailCo can evaluate. We would validate which signals store leaders trust, which Harbor Wiki content is being used, and where the replication model is strongest. We would also come back to scheduling as its own workstream. The discovery should tell us whether the next step is process redesign, system integration, workforce tooling, or a combination of those options.

slides.quote: I have no idea what actually happens on my shop floor. I get a spreadsheet on Monday about last week.
slides.script: We keep coming back to this quote because it captures the operating gap in one sentence. If leadership cannot see the shop floor until after the fact, the business is forced to manage through lagging indicators. That makes it difficult to coach, difficult to compare, and difficult to replicate excellence. Spacesight and Echo close that visibility gap, but the larger value comes when Harbor Wiki turns the learning into standards the stores can use. The goal is not more reporting. The goal is a faster loop from reality, to learning, to action.

slides.title: Our ask: a two-week discovery with Ops
slides.subtitle: Prove the replication model before scaling it
bullets: Select pilot stores and manager cohorts
Confirm Spacesight and Echo data access
slides.script: Our recommended next step is a focused two-week discovery with your operations team. We would use that time to choose the right pilot stores, confirm what Spacesight and Echo can capture, identify the managers whose practices we want to study, and map the onboarding and scheduling workflows honestly. At the end of the two weeks, we would have a clear 30, 60, and 90 day proposal built in Alivia. That gives RetailCo a practical way to test the core idea: the answers already exist in your best stores, and now we can replicate them.

approach.angle: The real problem is variance, not average performance. Argue that the customer already has the answers - they live in the best store managers - and the job is replication.
approach.device: Structure as 30 / 60 / 90 days - three horizons of what changes.
approach.opener: Open on the numbers of their operation, so the scale of the problem lands first.
approach.close: Close by asking for a two-week discovery with their ops team.
